data.title: THE PULLMAN STRIKE
data.subtitle: Pullman, Illinois — Summer 1894
data.introBody: May 1894. You are a skilled car-builder in the company town of Pullman, Illinois. George Pullman cut your wages by thirty percent. Your rent did not move. The arithmetic is simple and brutal. The American Railway Union is meeting tonight, and the men around you are deciding how far to push back.
data.trailFeedOpener: May 1894: the shop floor is quiet, but the anger underneath it isn't.

resourceLabels.standing: Standing in the Shop and the Street

events.title: The ARU Grievance Hearing, May 1894 — before the strike vote is called
events.text: Eugene Debs's committee has come to Pullman to hear workers describe the wage cuts and the unchanged rents. The foreman's informants are in the hall. Your name is on no list yet. The committee chair calls for anyone willing to speak on the record. Your wife is three months from delivering your second child. The man beside you — your closest friend on the shop floor — is already rising from his seat. The chair's eyes find yours.

choices.text: You rise and give your name. You describe, in plain numbers, what the Company took from your pay envelope and left on your rent bill.
choices.result: You have made yourself legible to the cause and to the Company both. You are no longer a private man managing a private crisis — you are a witness, and the record now holds your name.

choices.text: You hold your seat. You let your friend speak. You tell yourself his words carry the same facts yours would — and that your family cannot eat solidarity.
choices.result: You have drawn the line at your own threshold. The cause may still win or lose without your name on it, but you now know exactly where you stand — and so, quietly, does the man beside you.

events.title: Rent Day in a Company Town
events.text: The Pullman Company agent knocks on Tuesday morning. Rent is due — same as last month, same as the month before. Your paycheck this week is $6.07, of which $4.80 goes straight back to George Pullman. Your neighbor Maria got a check for two cents after deductions.

choices.text: Pay in full. Keep the roof.
choices.result: The agent marks you current. Your wife exhales. Down the block, three families got eviction notices instead.

choices.text: Pay half. Ask to negotiate arrears.
choices.result: The agent frowns and notes it in his ledger. You are not evicted — yet. The men in the hall hear you tried.

choices.text: Refuse to pay until wages match rent.
choices.result: Word spreads fast. Four other families on your block do the same thing by nightfall. The agent writes a name in a different ledger.

trivia: In Pullman's company town, workers paid rent directly to the Pullman Company — the same company that set their wages.
Some Pullman workers received paychecks of just two cents after rent and other company deductions were subtracted.

events.title: The Company Store
events.text: The only grocery in Pullman is the company store. Credit is running thin. A neighbor offers to walk with you to a shop in nearby Kensington — outside company property — but it is two miles and the foreman has been watching who leaves.

choices.text: Use the company store. Stay out of trouble.
choices.result: Prices are higher than Kensington but you stay current and unnoticed.

choices.text: Walk to Kensington with your neighbor.
choices.result: Flour is thirty cents cheaper per sack. The foreman says nothing — this time. You and your neighbor split the walk home.

choices.text: Organize a group buy in Kensington. Pool resources.
choices.result: Eight families send one person with pooled coin. It stretches further. The company agent notices the store is quieter.

trivia: Pullman's company town included a company-owned store, company-owned housing, and even a company-owned church.
Workers who lived in Pullman had no choice of landlord — George Pullman owned every building in the town.

events.title: The ARU Convention Vote, June 1894
events.text: Eugene Debs has called a vote at the ARU national convention in Chicago. If the union votes to refuse handling any train pulling Pullman cars, the boycott becomes national. Debs urges discipline — no violence, just refusal. The delegates are deciding right now.

choices.text: Support the boycott fully. Walk out with the ARU.
choices.result: The vote passes. Within days, ARU switchmen across twenty-seven states refuse to handle Pullman cars. Rail traffic grinds toward a halt. Your family asks how long the savings will last.

choices.text: Vote yes but keep a low profile afterward.
choices.result: You voted with the men but haven't put your name on anything. The boycott spreads without you at the front of it.

choices.text: Abstain. The boycott could destroy the union.
choices.result: Debs warned against half-measures. The men who abstained are noted. Your family is relieved. The shop floor is colder to you.

trivia: The ARU's boycott of Pullman cars began in late June 1894 and spread to railroad workers in twenty-seven states within days.
Eugene Debs asked ARU members to maintain the boycott peacefully — he believed disciplined refusal, not violence, was the union's strength.

events.title: Federal Troops Enter Chicago
events.text: President Grover Cleveland has ordered federal troops into Illinois over Governor Altgeld's written protest. Attorney General Richard Olney — a former railroad attorney — secured an injunction declaring the boycott an illegal conspiracy. ARU members who continue face arrest.

choices.text: Hold the line. Honor the boycott injunction or not.
choices.result: The troops fix bayonets on the rail yards. Debs is arrested within the week. You are still standing. So are fewer and fewer men beside you.

choices.text: Step back quietly. Protect the family.
choices.result: Your wife stops counting the days since you slept. The men who stayed out do not forget who stepped away when the troops came.

choices.text: Wait and see what the rest of the local does.
choices.result: Half the local waits with you. Half doesn't. By morning it doesn't matter — the injunction has already done its work.

trivia: Governor John Peter Altgeld formally protested Cleveland's deployment of federal troops into Illinois, arguing it violated state authority.
Richard Olney used the Sherman Anti-Trust Act — passed to break up corporations — as the legal basis for the injunction against the ARU strike.

events.title: A Quiet Word from the Foreman
events.text: The floor foreman pulls you aside between shifts. The company wants names — ARU organizers, men who refused to cross. He implies those who cooperate will be first rehired when this ends. He leaves the offer open.

choices.text: Refuse. Say nothing.
choices.result: The foreman nods and walks away. Nothing happens today. Whether nothing happens tomorrow depends on how long you can hold.

choices.text: Give a vague non-answer. Buy time.
choices.result: You say enough to seem cooperative, nothing specific. It works for now. You feel it settle into something you will need to carry.

choices.text: Give a name. Just one. Someone already arrested.
choices.result: The foreman writes it down. You get a small advance on back pay. On the block that night, something in the way men look at you has changed.

events.title: The Strike Breaks — What Do You Do Now?
events.text: The ARU has voted to end the boycott. Debs is in prison. The railroads are running again with replacement workers. The Pullman Company is accepting applications — but only from men who sign a loyalty oath swearing they are not ARU members. Your family has three weeks of larder left.

choices.text: Sign the oath. Take the work. Feed the family.
choices.result: You sign. Your name goes into the company ledger as compliant. Your wife does not ask what you signed. The men who didn't sign will be blacklisted across every railroad in the country. You will see their faces at church.

choices.text: Refuse the oath. Accept blacklisting.
choices.result: Your name goes on the blacklist. Every major railroad in America will have it. You do not know yet how long hungry lasts or where the next work comes from. You know you did not sign.

choices.text: Leave Pullman. Find work in another city.
choices.result: You pack what fits in two bags. The town shrinks behind you. Whatever happened here, you were part of it — and now you are gone from it.

events.title: The night the strike vote passes and the boycott is called — the shop floor empties and the men look to one another

text.default: When the hands go up and the vote carries, the men around you look to you the way men look to someone who already has skin in the game. You spoke first. You are not being asked whether you will honor the strike — you are being asked where you will stand on the picket line and who you will talk to when the new men come off the train. You made yourself a leader the day you gave your name, and the strike has simply revealed what that means.

variants.text: When the hands go up and the vote carries, the men around you look to you the way men look to someone who already has skin in the game. You spoke first. You are not being asked whether you will honor the strike — you are being asked where you will stand on the picket line and who you will talk to when the new men come off the train. You made yourself a leader the day you gave your name, and the strike has simply revealed what that means.

When the hands go up and the vote carries, the room is loud with it — and you are loud with it too. But your friend does not meet your eye right away, and in that pause you understand that he is deciding something about you, the same way you decided something about yourself at the hearing. You will honor the strike. But there is a difference between a man who strikes because he must and a man who struck because he chose to first, and the men in this room have begun to feel it.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Eugene V. Debs
sages.title: President, American Railway Union
sages.bio: Eugene V. Debs founded the American Railway Union in 1893 — the first industrial union to organize all railroad workers regardless of craft. He led the Pullman boycott and was arrested under a federal injunction. He later ran for president five times as a socialist, once from a prison cell.
sages.greeting: Debs speaks to a packed union hall in Chicago. His voice carries the kind of conviction that makes men feel less afraid.
sages.advice: "Gentlemen, this is not a strike against wages. It is a strike against the system that took your wages while keeping your rent. An injury to one is the concern of all."

question.question: What made the ARU's boycott unusually powerful compared to earlier railroad strikes?
choices: It was organized by craft — only skilled workers participated
It was an industrial union — all railroad workers across crafts refused Pullman cars together
It was backed by federal troops from the start
It focused only on the Pullman company town, not the railroads
question.explanation: Older railroad unions organized by craft — engineers in one union, firemen in another. Debs's ARU organized all railroad workers together as one industrial union, which meant a single boycott vote could paralyze rail traffic across twenty-seven states at once.
question.teksRef: 8.22(A) — Labor organization and the rise of industrial unionism in the Gilded Age

sages.name: John Peter Altgeld
sages.title: Governor of Illinois
sages.bio: John Peter Altgeld was the Democratic Governor of Illinois and one of the few prominent politicians who openly sympathized with labor. He had already pardoned the surviving Haymarket defendants. When Cleveland sent federal troops into Illinois without his request, Altgeld wrote a formal protest — one of the strongest statements of states' rights and labor sympathy of the era.
sages.greeting: A copy of Governor Altgeld's letter to President Cleveland is circulating in the hall. A delegate reads it aloud.
sages.advice: "The Governor says the President had no legal authority to send troops into Illinois without a state request. He says the real reason was not mail delivery — it was breaking the union."

question.question: Why did Governor Altgeld formally protest President Cleveland's decision?
choices: He wanted federal troops sent sooner
He believed Cleveland had no authority to send troops into Illinois without the state's request
He wanted the Pullman Company to be nationalized
He opposed the ARU boycott and wanted state troops used instead
question.explanation: Altgeld argued that deploying federal troops inside a state without the governor's request violated the constitutional relationship between federal and state authority. He believed Cleveland used the pretext of protecting mail delivery to crush the strike on behalf of the railroads.
question.teksRef: 8.20(B) — Federalism and the limits of federal authority in the Gilded Age

sages.name: George Pullman
sages.title: Founder, Pullman Palace Car Company
sages.bio: George Pullman built his fortune manufacturing luxury sleeping cars for American railroads, then built the town of Pullman, Illinois as a controlled model community for his workers. He owned the homes, the stores, and the church. When the depression of 1893 hit, he cut wages but not rents. He refused every request to negotiate and never returned to the town after the strike.
sages.greeting: A company pamphlet is passed around the hall — Pullman's public statement defending his conduct. Someone reads it with visible contempt.
sages.advice: "He says the town is a model of industrial order. He says the wage cuts were a business necessity. He says there is nothing to arbitrate."

question.question: What did George Pullman own in the town of Pullman that gave him total control over his workers' daily lives?
choices: The railroad lines and the locomotives
The workers' union contracts and their wages only
The homes, the stores, and the church
The city government of Chicago
question.explanation: Pullman owned every building in the company town — including the workers' homes, the company store where they bought groceries, and even the church. This meant workers paid rent, bought food, and worshipped all at the pleasure of the same man who set their wages.
question.teksRef: 8.22(B) — Company towns and employer control of labor in the Gilded Age

Pullman cut wages but did not lower rents in the company town

It was an industrial union organizing all railroad workers together

Break up large business monopolies and trusts
Authorize federal troops in labor disputes
Set minimum wage standards
eventTrivia.fact: Congress passed the Sherman Anti-Trust Act to curb corporate monopolies, but in 1894 the Cleveland administration turned it against the ARU, arguing the boycott was an illegal 'combination in restraint of trade.'

choices: It agreed to negotiate wages but not rents
It refused all arbitration, saying there was nothing to discuss
It raised wages by ten percent as a compromise
It asked the ARU to mediate
eventTrivia.fact: George Pullman refused every request for arbitration or negotiation, insisting the wage cuts were a business necessity and that his conduct of the company was not subject to outside review.

choices: Protecting ARU members from violence
Ensuring the delivery of U.S. mail
Preventing a socialist revolution
Supporting Governor Altgeld's request
eventTrivia.fact: Cleveland justified federal intervention by arguing that the rail stoppage was obstructing U.S. mail delivery, giving the federal government a constitutional hook to act without the state's invitation.

A list of union organizers shared among railroads to prevent their rehiring
A court order against striking workers
A federal register of dangerous railroads
eventTrivia.fact: After the strike, the General Managers' Association — which represented the major railroads — maintained a blacklist of ARU members and organizers, effectively barring them from employment across the industry.

choices: The Panic of 1873
The Depression of 1893
The Recession of 1887
The Financial Crisis of 1900
eventTrivia.fact: The economic depression that began with the Panic of 1893 caused Pullman's orders to fall sharply. He responded by cutting wages — but used the same depression as a reason not to cut rents, since his shareholders still expected returns.

eventTrivia.question: What was the General Managers' Association?
choices: A federal agency overseeing railroads
A labor union for railroad managers
A coalition of railroad companies that coordinated to break the boycott
A congressional committee on labor
eventTrivia.fact: The General Managers' Association represented twenty-four Chicago railroads. It coordinated the industry's response to the ARU boycott — firing workers who honored it, hiring replacements, and lobbying for federal intervention.

eventTrivia.question: What did Debs believe was the key discipline that would make the boycott succeed?
choices: Armed self-defense at the rail yards
Peaceful refusal — no violence, just a refusal to handle Pullman cars
Negotiating secretly with Pullman
Winning a court injunction before the railroads did
eventTrivia.fact: Debs consistently urged ARU members to maintain the boycott through peaceful, non-violent refusal — he knew that any violence would give the government and the press justification for suppression.

data.historicalContext: The Pullman Strike of 1894 began when the Pullman Palace Car Company cut wages by up to thirty percent without reducing rents in the company town it owned outright. When Pullman refused all arbitration, the American Railway Union voted to boycott Pullman cars nationwide. The strike spread to twenty-seven states and nearly paralyzed American rail traffic. President Cleveland deployed federal troops over Governor Altgeld's formal protest; Attorney General Olney obtained a sweeping injunction under the Sherman Anti-Trust Act. Eugene Debs was arrested and imprisoned. The strike was broken, approximately thirty people died in related violence, and the railroads blacklisted thousands of ARU members. Debs served six months in prison and emerged a committed socialist. The strike is remembered as a turning point in the relationship between federal power and organized labor.

verdict.good: You testified. You held the line when the troops came. You refused the oath at the end. You knew what it would cost — the blacklist, the empty larder, the look on your wife's face — and you paid it. The strike broke anyway. Debs went to prison. The company won, the way the company always won in 1894. Thirty people died and the railroads kept running. But the men who came after you — in 1935 when the Wagner Act passed, in 1937 when the sit-down strikers won — stood on the ground you refused to give up. You lost. It mattered.
verdict.bad: Every time the choice came, you found a reason that wasn't quite cowardice — the baby coming, the larder, the roof. You gave the foreman a name. You signed the oath. You kept the paycheck and the house. Nobody can say you were cruel. The men on the blacklist, the ones who ate nothing for weeks because they wouldn't give a name — they lost, and you didn't. You were on the right side of the ledger in 1894. You were on the wrong side of everything else. The strike broke, and you helped it break.
verdict.indifferent: You abstained, waited, and watched for which way the wind was blowing, and then followed it. Not the company, not the union — the exit. The strike happened around you. Federal troops marched past you. Debs went to prison while you kept your head down. Thirty people died in those rail yards, and you were there, and you have nothing to say about it. History does not record where you stood during the Pullman Strike. You couldn't either.

data.reviewSummary:
In the spring of 1894, George Pullman cut his workers' wages by up to thirty percent but refused to lower rents in the company town of Pullman, Illinois — a town where he owned the homes, the stores, and the church. Some workers received paychecks of just two cents after deductions. When Pullman refused all arbitration, workers turned to Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union. The ARU was different from earlier railroad unions, which organized by craft — engineers in one union, firemen in another. The ARU was an industrial union that organized all railroad workers together, which meant a single boycott vote could paralyze rail traffic across twenty-seven states. In late June 1894, ARU members voted to refuse to handle any train pulling Pullman cars. The boycott spread rapidly and nearly shut down American rail traffic.

President Grover Cleveland's administration moved to break the strike. Attorney General Richard Olney — a former railroad attorney — obtained a sweeping federal injunction by turning the Sherman Anti-Trust Act, originally passed to break up business monopolies, against the labor union instead. Cleveland then ordered federal troops into Illinois over the written protest of Governor John Peter Altgeld, who argued the President had no authority to send troops into a state without the governor's request, and that the real purpose was crushing the union under the pretext of protecting mail delivery.

Debs was arrested for violating the injunction and served six months in prison, where he became a committed socialist. The strike collapsed. The Pullman Company and the railroads, coordinated through the General Managers' Association, hired replacement workers and required returning employees to sign loyalty oaths swearing they were not ARU members. Those who refused were placed on a blacklist shared across the industry, barring them from railroad work. Approximately thirty people died in strike-related violence. The Pullman Strike became a defining moment in the history of American labor — demonstrating both the power of industrial unionism and the willingness of federal government to intervene on behalf of property and commerce.

data.title: 381 DAYS
data.subtitle: Montgomery, Alabama, 1955–1956
data.introBody: December 1955, Montgomery, Alabama. Rosa Parks has been arrested for refusing to give up her seat. The Black community is calling for a boycott of the city buses — starting Monday. You ride that bus every day to get to your job across town. Starting tomorrow, you walk.
data.trailFeedOpener: Monday morning, December 5, 1955: the buses roll past empty. You tighten your coat and start walking.

events.title: Week Two of the Boycott — The Church-Step Moment
events.text: The mass meeting at Dexter Avenue Baptist has just ended and the air is still ringing. Reverend Abernathy's aide stops you on the church steps and asks you directly: they are compiling a community witness list — names of ordinary riders willing to be counted publicly, to show the White Citizens' Council that it isn't just Rosa Parks, it's everyone. Your name on that list means your employer will likely see it. It also means the neighbor standing next to you doesn't carry the whole weight alone. He waits. You answer.

choices.text: You give your name. You say it clearly, and he writes it down.
choices.result: You have decided that the community's need to be seen outweighs the protection of your own household. You have made the boycott personal and public in a way that cannot be undone.

choices.text: You shake your head and tell him you can't — not your name, not now. You turn and walk home in the dark.
choices.result: You have decided that what you owe the people under your roof outweighs what you owe the people on that list. You will carry the boycott in your feet and your silence, and carry the cost of that choice inside yourself.

events.title: First Monday — The Long Walk
events.text: The buses are almost empty. Hundreds of Black workers are walking, some four miles each way in the cold. Your feet ache by noon, but the streets feel different — purposeful. Your employer watches you arrive late and asks pointed questions.

choices.text: Tell her plainly: you support the boycott.
choices.result: She gives you a hard look. You hold it. Your neighbor on the walk home squeezes your arm — word travels fast.

choices.text: Say your regular ride fell through. Keep quiet.
choices.result: She seems satisfied. You keep your job for now, but the half-truth sits in your chest the rest of the day.

choices.text: Apologize, promise to be on time. Don't explain.
choices.result: She lets it go. You let it go too. Another day without a line drawn.

events.title: The Carpool Collection Tin
events.text: The MIA has set up a carpool network — Black-owned cars making routes the buses used to run. But fuel and drivers cost money. Deacon Willis passes the tin at church. You have precious little, but so does everyone.

choices.text: Give a full week's bus fare to the tin.
choices.result: You ride the carpool all week. The woman beside you gives you half her biscuit without a word.

choices.text: Drop in a small coin — something at least.
choices.result: Enough to hold your head up. The carpool list includes your street.

choices.text: Pass the tin along. Rent is due.
choices.result: You keep your coins. The next week the carpool route skips your block.

events.title: Pulled Over on Ripley Street
events.text: A police cruiser pulls alongside your carpool. Commissioner Sellers has ordered his officers to fine carpool drivers for any pretext — expired tags, improper turns, loitering. The driver grips the wheel. You see the officer's hand on his door handle.

choices.text: Stay calm, say nothing, let the driver handle it.
choices.result: The officer writes a ticket for a cracked tail light that wasn't cracked before. You all pay a share of the fine.

choices.text: Speak up: ask the officer to state the violation.
choices.result: He issues a second citation — disturbing the peace. It costs you. But the driver later says it was the bravest thing he'd seen all month.

choices.text: Slip out the far door and walk the rest.
choices.result: You avoid the fine but walk two miles in the rain. Your shoes won't dry until Tuesday.

events.title: Mass Meeting at Dexter Avenue
events.text: Reverend King is speaking tonight. The church is packed past the windows, voices answering him back. The MIA needs people to help staff the information table — names taken, rides coordinated. But staffing the table means your name goes on a list the police will try to get.

choices.text: Staff the table. Put your name down.
choices.result: Two dozen people sign up for rides because you were there. You walk home with something warm in your chest — and a chill at your back.

choices.text: Attend and sing, but don't staff the table.
choices.result: The singing fills you up. You are part of it — at the margins, but present.

choices.text: Stay home. Rest your feet.
choices.result: You sleep well. In the morning you hear what you missed, second-hand.

events.title: The Morning After the Bombing
events.text: Reverend King's house was bombed last night. His wife and baby were inside; they survived. Hundreds of Black residents gathered outside, some armed. King came to the porch and asked everyone to go home peacefully. Your block is tense and afraid. A young man on the corner says the time for nonviolence is over.

choices.text: Agree with King. Urge calm on the corner.
choices.result: It costs you the young man's respect. Three others nod quietly. The block stays calm.

choices.text: Stay silent. Let others decide.
choices.result: The corner argument continues past midnight. Nothing breaks, but nothing holds either.

choices.text: Tell the young man he's right — enough patience.
choices.result: He grips your hand. But the MIA's discipline is the boycott's armor, and you just put a crack in it.

events.title: November 13 — The Supreme Court Rules
events.text: Word comes: the Supreme Court has struck down Alabama's bus segregation laws. The boycott is over — won. The MIA asks everyone who participated to ride the first integrated buses together, visibly, as a community. Your employer has already warned you that showing up in the newspaper will cost you your job.

choices.text: Board the first integrated bus. Ride openly.
choices.result: The bus is quiet with something enormous. You sit where you want. You lose your job the next week. You do not regret it.

choices.text: Ride alone later, quietly — no cameras.
choices.result: You ride. You feel it. No one photographs you, and your employer hears nothing. But you know who carried the front.

choices.text: Skip it. Keep your head down, protect the job.
choices.result: You watch from the window as the first buses roll past integrated. The wages stay in your pocket. The distance in your neighbors' eyes costs more.

events.title: Month Three — Your Employer Calls You In

text.default: Your employer sets a newspaper clipping on the desk between you. Your name is in the third paragraph. She says she has always considered you reliable, and she hopes you understand the position this puts her in. You understand it perfectly. You understood it on the church steps. The question now is whether the thing you chose then still feels like yours — and it does, and it costs exactly what you knew it would cost.

sages.name: Jo Ann Robinson
sages.title: Women's Political Council President
sages.bio: Jo Ann Robinson was a professor at Alabama State College and president of the Women's Political Council. The night of Rosa Parks's arrest, she stayed up until dawn printing and folding 52,500 boycott flyers, which WPC members distributed across Black Montgomery by morning.
sages.greeting: A woman at your church hands you a mimeographed flyer before dawn. You recognize her — Jo Ann Robinson, from the college. She's been up all night.
sages.advice: "We didn't wait for permission. We had the mimeo machine and we had the night. By morning, every Black school, barbershop, and beauty salon in this city will know." She presses a stack of flyers into your arms.

question.question: What did Jo Ann Robinson do the night Rosa Parks was arrested?
choices: She organized a march on City Hall
She printed and distributed 52,500 boycott flyers by morning
She filed a federal lawsuit against the bus company
She called a press conference for national newspapers
question.explanation: Robinson and the Women's Political Council printed 52,500 flyers overnight on December 1–2, 1955, calling for a one-day boycott on December 5. This grassroots infrastructure — already in place before Parks's arrest — made mass participation possible from the very first day.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.29(A) — Civic participation and the role of organized community action in the Civil Rights Movement

sages.name: E.D. Nixon
sages.title: NAACP Chapter Leader & Pullman Porter
sages.bio: E.D. Nixon was the head of the Montgomery NAACP and a Pullman railroad porter. He bailed Rosa Parks out of jail, recognized her case as the one to fight, and convened the Black ministers and leaders whose meeting produced the Montgomery Improvement Association — and elected King as its president.
sages.greeting: You find E.D. Nixon at the Dexter Avenue steps after the mass meeting, still in his porter's uniform, hat in hand.
sages.advice: "Parks wasn't the first to refuse. But she was the right person — respectable, calm, NAACP-trained. A movement needs its moment, and its moment needs the right person in the seat."

question.question: Why did E.D. Nixon consider Rosa Parks the right person to challenge bus segregation in court?
choices: She was a city employee and could not be fired
She was an NAACP member with an impeccable reputation, making her a strong legal test case
She had previously won a lawsuit against the bus company
She was related to a federal judge who supported civil rights
question.explanation: Nixon and NAACP attorney Clifford Durr knew that a court challenge required a plaintiff with an unimpeachable character. Parks was a trained NAACP secretary, calm under pressure, and without a legal record — qualities that made her an ideal plaintiff and a figure the White community could not easily dismiss.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.29(B) — Strategies and turning points of the Civil Rights Movement

sages.name: Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.
sages.title: President, Montgomery Improvement Association
sages.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. was a 26-year-old pastor at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church when he was elected president of the Montgomery Improvement Association. He led the boycott's public voice, synthesizing Gandhian nonviolence with the Black church tradition into a disciplined movement strategy.
sages.greeting: After a mass meeting, Reverend King stops to speak with people at the door. He looks you in the eye, unhurried, as though there is no bomb threat waiting for him at home.
sages.advice: "Our weapon is not the brick. It is the empty seat. Every Black man and woman who walks to work is a vote no politician in this city can ignore. Stay nonviolent. Stay united. The law is coming around to us."

question.question: What legal ruling ended the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
choices: The Alabama Supreme Court ordered the city to negotiate with the MIA
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that bus segregation in Alabama was unconstitutional
The federal government threatened to cut Montgomery's highway funding
The bus company agreed to integrate voluntarily to end its financial losses
question.explanation: In November 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower federal court ruling in Browder v. Gayle, declaring Alabama's bus segregation laws unconstitutional. The boycott officially ended on December 20, 1956 — 381 days after it began — when integrated buses resumed service.

eventTrivia.fact: White employers, landlords, and the White Citizens' Council applied coordinated economic pressure: workers faced job loss, tenants faced eviction, and insurance policies were cancelled — making daily participation in the boycott a genuine financial sacrifice.

data.historicalContext: The Montgomery Bus Boycott lasted 381 days, from December 5, 1955 to December 20, 1956. Roughly 40,000 Black bus riders — domestic workers, teachers, students — walked, carpooled, and sacrificed to sustain the pressure. The campaign succeeded: the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Alabama bus segregation unconstitutional in Browder v. Gayle. It launched Martin Luther King Jr. as a national figure and proved that disciplined, organized nonviolent direct action could defeat institutionalized segregation — a model the wider Civil Rights Movement would carry forward for a decade.

verdict.good: You walked. You gave when you had little to give. You said your name when saying it was dangerous. The boycott won — 381 days of empty buses and the Supreme Court agreed with what you knew from the start. But history didn't win it for you. The people on that sidewalk every morning did, and you were one of them. That cost something real, and you paid it.
verdict.bad: You kept your wages. You kept your seat at work. You kept your head below every parapet that mattered. The boycott won anyway — the Supreme Court ruled, the buses integrated, King's name went into the history books. You were there for all of it and put nothing in. The people who walked four miles in bad shoes before dawn won a thing you'll spend the rest of your life benefiting from. They carried you. You never carried them.
verdict.indifferent: You moved through 381 days without quite deciding anything. Not for the boycott, not against it — just adjacent to it, letting the current take you where it went. The boycott won. Montgomery integrated its buses. History turned, and you were standing nearby when it did. But the question every ordinary person in Montgomery had to answer — what do I owe the people walking beside me? — you deferred it every time until it expired. You passed through one of the most consequential years in American history. It asked something of you. You found a way to not quite hear the question.

data.reviewSummary: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks — an NAACP secretary and seamstress — was arrested on a Montgomery city bus for refusing to give her seat to a white passenger. That night, Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council printed 52,500 flyers calling for a one-day boycott on December 5, distributing them to churches, schools, barbershops, and beauty salons across Black Montgomery before morning. E.D. Nixon, the NAACP chapter leader and Pullman porter who bailed Parks out of jail, recognized her as an ideal plaintiff: calm, trained, and with an impeccable reputation that made her a strong legal test case. Black leaders met and formed the Montgomery Improvement Association, electing 26-year-old Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. as its president. The boycott that was supposed to last one day lasted 381 days. Roughly 40,000 Black riders — domestic workers, teachers, students — walked, carpooled, and sacrificed daily. The MIA organized a network of Black-owned cars to replace the buses, funded by community collections. Commissioner Clyde Sellers, a White Citizens' Council member, directed police to fine carpool drivers on any available pretext to break the network. Employers fired workers, landlords threatened eviction, and the White Citizens' Council applied coordinated economic pressure against participants. On January 30, 1956, King's home was bombed while his wife Coretta and their baby were inside; both survived. King came to his porch and urged the crowd of armed, angry neighbors to go home peacefully, holding the movement's nonviolent discipline at its most dangerous moment. The legal challenge came through Browder v. Gayle, filed by four Black women plaintiffs. The federal district court ruled Alabama bus segregation unconstitutional; the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed that ruling on November 13, 1956. Integrated bus service resumed on December 20, 1956 — 381 days after the boycott began — and the movement that proved nonviolent direct action could defeat institutionalized segregation carried that lesson forward into the decade ahead.

data.title: STAR-SPANGLED DUTY
data.subtitle: A Young Militiaman in the War of 1812
data.introBody: Summer, 1812. You are a state militiaman called up from your county — a farmer's son with a musket, a knapsack, and a few dollars sewn into your coat lining. The British are pressing American sailors into their navy, the frontier is on fire, and Congress has just declared war. Your neighbors are watching to see what kind of man you are.
data.trailFeedOpener: Summer 1812: the muster drum sounds across the county and you fall in with your neighbors.

events.title: Early campaign — the morning the column forms up to cross the state line in answer to a federal call for reinforcement
events.text: Your company has been mustered for home defense. The federal officer reads the order: regulars are stretched thin, the enemy column is moving, and your militia is needed across the border now. Your captain says the choice is yours — the law is genuinely unclear, some of your men are already falling in, and one older sergeant quietly reminds you that your enlistment says 'defense of this state.' Your family's farm is two days' ride behind you. The column is about to step off.

choices.text: Shoulder your musket and fall in with the column. The line on the map means less than the men beside you.
choices.result: He is someone who, at the decisive moment, let solidarity and a larger conception of duty override the shelter the law offered him — a man who will measure himself afterward by what the crossing cost, not just by whether it succeeded.

choices.text: Step out of line and stand fast. Your enlistment is for this state, your family is unguarded, and you will not be shamed for holding to what you promised.
choices.result: He is someone who, at the decisive moment, held the boundary of his obligation as a real thing rather than a convenient excuse — a man who will measure himself afterward by whether that boundary was principle or self-protection, and may never fully know.

events.title: Empty Haversack
events.text: The supply wagon hasn't come in four days. Your rations are gone and the regulars in camp are hoarding what little flour is left. A neighbor in your company has nothing at all.

choices.text: Share your last hardtack with the neighbor.
choices.result: He eats. You go hungry another day. Your stomach tightens but your conscience doesn't. He remembers.

choices.text: Spend coin to buy food from a sutler.
choices.result: A dollar buys a loaf and a strip of salted pork. You eat alone and feel almost human again.

choices.text: Go without. Save the coin.
choices.result: You keep the coin for home. By nightfall you can barely lift your pack. The neighbor watches you struggle and says nothing.

image.artist: Clockwise, from top: George Munger, John David Kelly, Anton Otto Fischer, William Emmons, Edward Percy Moran

events.title: Cracked Flintlock
events.text: Your musket's frizzen has cracked — the flint won't spark reliably. The army quartermaster has spare parts but demands a favor: carry his private letter to an officer two miles off, delaying your own duties.

choices.text: Run the letter. Get the part.
choices.result: The frizzen fits clean. Your musket snaps fire on the first strike. The favor cost you an afternoon but it was worth it.

choices.text: Pay a blacksmith from your own coin.
choices.result: Three shillings and an hour wait. The repair is solid and you owe no one anything. But that money was meant for home.

choices.text: Tie a rag around it and hope.
choices.result: It misfires twice at the next drill. An officer notices and moves you to the rear rank. Your messmates shake their heads.

events.title: The Capital Is Burning
events.text: August 1814. Admiral Cockburn's redcoats have marched into Washington unopposed and put the Capitol and the President's House to the torch. Your company is on the road from Maryland — too late to stop it. The road is choked with fleeing civilians. A woman says Dolley Madison got out with the Gilbert Stuart portrait of Washington and the government papers, but the city is lost.
trivia: Admiral George Cockburn personally supervised the burning of Washington's public buildings in August 1814.
Dolley Madison rescued the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington and key government papers before fleeing the White House.
The British burned the Capitol, the White House, and other federal buildings — a deliberate act meant to humiliate the young republic.

choices.text: Help civilians carry their belongings to safety.
choices.result: You haul an old man's trunk three miles before collapsing at the roadside. He grips your hand. The city smells of smoke for two days.

choices.text: Stay with your company. Keep rank.
choices.result: Discipline holds. Your sergeant nods. The civilians manage. You march through ash and broken glass and say nothing.

choices.text: Slip away and check on kin in the area.
choices.result: You find your cousin's household untouched and leave a coin for their trouble. Your company has moved on without you. You catch up the next morning, mud on your boots and no excuse ready.

events.title: The Night the Rockets Flew
events.text: September 13, 1814. The British fleet pounds Fort McHenry through the night with rockets and bombshells. You are dug in on the Baltimore shore, watching the sky light up. A man named Francis Scott Key is out there on a British ship, having gone to negotiate a prisoner's release — now he can only watch and wait like the rest of us.
trivia: Francis Scott Key watched the bombardment of Fort McHenry from a British ship where he had gone to negotiate the release of an American prisoner.
The British fired Congreve rockets and bombshells at Fort McHenry for 25 hours. The fort held.
Key wrote the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner' after seeing the American flag still flying at dawn.

choices.text: Hold your post all night without sleep.
choices.result: By dawn your eyes ache and your hands shake, but the flag is still up there. You feel something you can't name yet.

choices.text: Rotate with a messmate — four hours each.
choices.result: Sensible. You each get a stretch of sleep. The rockets keep coming either way.

choices.text: Pull back to a covered position and rest.
choices.result: You tell yourself a tired soldier is no good to anyone. Probably true. The man who held your spot doesn't speak to you at breakfast.

image.artist: Original uploader was Dr.frog at en.wikipedia

events.title: Fever in the Tent
events.text: Your tent mate has camp fever — shaking chills, yellow skin. The regimental surgeon is three miles off and camp medicine is nearly gone. Staying to nurse him means missing the next muster. Going to muster means leaving him alone.

choices.text: Stay and nurse him through the worst of it.
choices.result: You spend coin on broth and strip your own coat to keep him warm. He pulls through. He will owe you a debt he can never pay, and he knows it.

choices.text: Go to muster; tell the surgeon on the way.
choices.result: You flag down a surgeon's aide. He gets to the man by evening. Not the same as staying, but not nothing.

choices.text: Go to muster. He's not your responsibility.
choices.result: He survives — barely. When he's on his feet again he doesn't meet your eyes. Some things don't need to be said aloud.

events.title: The Road Back
events.text: Word comes that the Treaty of Ghent has been signed and peace is declared. Your muster is up. The road home is open — but your captain asks for two more weeks of volunteers to help clear Baltimore's defenses and tend the wounded still in the hospital tents. Your family hasn't had a letter in three months.

choices.text: Volunteer the two weeks. See the duty through.
choices.result: You write a short note home and stay. The men in the hospital tents are strangers, but they are yours now. When you finally walk back up your own lane your wife counts the days without saying a word.

choices.text: Head home. Your family needs you more.
choices.result: You fold your kit and go. The road is long and your boots are worn through, but your children are in the doorway before you reach the gate. You told yourself the war was done — and it was, for you.

choices.text: Ask what others in your company are doing.
choices.result: Half stay, half go. You follow the majority. It felt like a decision; it wasn't really.

events.title: After the battle — survivors return and the town holds a public gathering to account for who served where

You defended something. You are not certain what it cost everyone else.

sages.name: Henry Clay
sages.title: Speaker of the House; War Hawk

portraitAttribution.artist: Julian Vannerson or Montgomery P. Simons

sages.bio: Henry Clay of Kentucky became Speaker of the House in 1811 and led the War Hawks — a faction of young congressmen who demanded war with Britain over impressment, frontier raids, and national honor. His oratory transformed outrage into legislation.
sages.greeting: A congressman's aide finds you at muster and hands you a pamphlet. The man himself is speaking to a crowd nearby — Clay, loud as a camp auctioneer, gesturing at the sky.
sages.advice: "Britain seizes our sailors in open water and calls it law. The frontier burns while London arms the tribes against us. A nation that will not fight for its sailors is no nation at all."

question.question: What was the main reason War Hawks like Henry Clay demanded war with Britain in 1812?
choices: Britain had blocked all American trade with France
Britain was impressing American sailors and supporting frontier tribes against U.S. settlers
Britain had refused to return land seized in the Revolution
Britain had attacked an American naval base in the Caribbean
question.explanation: War Hawks were outraged by British impressment of American sailors — forcing them to serve on Royal Navy ships — and by British support for Native American tribes resisting U.S. expansion on the frontier. These twin grievances drove Congress toward the declaration of war in June 1812.
question.teksRef: 8.5(A) — Causes of the War of 1812 including impressment and frontier conflict

sages.name: Francis Scott Key
sages.title: American Lawyer; Witness to Fort McHenry
sages.bio: Francis Scott Key was a Georgetown lawyer who boarded a British ship in September 1814 to negotiate the release of an American prisoner. Detained overnight during the bombardment of Fort McHenry, he watched through the night and wrote the poem that became the national anthem.
sages.greeting: A pale, tired-looking man in a civilian coat finds your fire after the bombardment ends. He has ink on his fingers and keeps looking back toward the harbor.
sages.advice: "I was their prisoner all night — watching. Every burst of those rockets, I did not know if the fort still stood. When the dawn came and the flag was there — I had to write it down."

question.question: Why was Francis Scott Key on a British ship during the bombardment of Fort McHenry?
choices: He was a British spy reporting on American defenses
He had gone to negotiate the release of an American prisoner and was detained
He was a Royal Navy surgeon treating wounded sailors
He was delivering a peace offer from President Madison
question.explanation: Key went to the British fleet under a flag of truce to negotiate the release of an American civilian, Dr. William Beanes. The British agreed to free Beanes but held Key on the ship during the bombardment so he could not report on their plans. His overnight vigil produced the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner.'
question.teksRef: 8.5(B) — Key events of the War of 1812 including the defense of Baltimore and Fort McHenry

sages.name: Andrew Jackson
sages.title: Major General, U.S. Army; Victor at New Orleans
sages.bio: Andrew Jackson led a mixed force of regulars, militia, free Black soldiers, and pirates to a stunning victory over a veteran British army at the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815 — two weeks after the peace treaty had already been signed. The battle made him a national hero and shaped the myth of what the war had won.
sages.greeting: You hear him before you see him — a rail-thin Tennessee general with a jaw like a rifle stock, telling a circle of soldiers what the war meant.
sages.advice: "The treaty was signed before we fired a shot at New Orleans. No matter. Those redcoats came to take this city, and they learned something about American soldiers that day that London will not soon forget."

question.question: What is most historically significant about the Battle of New Orleans?
choices: It forced Britain to sign the Treaty of Ghent and end the war
It was fought after the peace treaty was already signed, yet became the war's defining symbol of American victory
It was the largest naval battle of the war, fought in the Gulf of Mexico
It secured American control of the Mississippi River for the first time
question.explanation: The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, ended the war before the Battle of New Orleans was fought on January 8, 1815. News traveled slowly, so neither side knew. The battle — a lopsided American victory — became the war's most famous moment and made Jackson a national hero, powerfully shaping the public memory of what the war had achieved.

data.historicalContext: The War of 1812 lasted from June 1812 to February 1815. The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, restored prewar boundaries and settled none of the war's stated causes — Britain never formally renounced impressment. Yet the war's legacy was enormous: the defense of Fort McHenry produced the national anthem, Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans became the founding myth of a new American nationalism, and the young republic had fought the world's greatest military power to a draw. For the militiamen who served, it was a war of supply failures, contested legal obligations, and hard choices made far from home.

verdict.good: You carried more than your share, and it showed. When the rations ran out you gave yours away; when the column needed bodies on the line you were there. It cost you — in coin, in sleep, in the look on your wife's face when you finally came home late. The war ended the way it usually ends between great powers and small ones: a treaty that settled nothing, a flag still flying over a battered fort, and a country that told itself it had won. You did not win anything you can hold. But the men who stood next to you knew who you were, and so do you.
verdict.bad: Every time the choice came, you took the one that kept you whole. The coin stayed in your pocket, the post got covered by someone else, the sick man managed without you. You are not a villain — you are a man who looked at each fork in the road and took the one with less mud. The flag flew. The treaty was signed. You came home in better shape than most. The men who gave more than you did came home to the same peace. You can tell yourself that was the sensible thing. It was. It was also a choice, made over and over, that left someone else holding the weight.
verdict.indifferent: You passed through the war like water through a sieve — present, going through the motions, never quite committing to anything. When the choices were hard you waited for them to simplify, and they mostly did, because someone else decided first. The capital burned. The rockets flew over the harbor. Your messmates held or broke or went home early, and you followed whichever way the group moved. The Treaty of Ghent was signed and you were mustered out and you went home, and the war happened around you the whole time. History didn't ask much of you. You didn't offer much either.

data.reviewSummary:
The War of 1812 began in June 1812 after years of failed diplomacy. Britain had been impressing American sailors — seizing them from merchant vessels and forcing them to serve on Royal Navy warships — and supporting Native American tribes resisting U.S. expansion on the frontier. War Hawks in Congress, led by Speaker Henry Clay of Kentucky, pushed President James Madison to act. Madison had tried embargoes and negotiations for years before War Hawk pressure and accumulated grievances left him no political alternative, and he reluctantly asked Congress for a declaration of war.

For state militiamen, the war meant supply failures, contested orders, and choices far from home. Their enlistments were written for defense of their home state, making federal orders to cross state lines legally and constitutionally disputed — a genuine fault line the republic argued over for decades.

The war's most dramatic moments came in the summer and autumn of 1814. In August, a British force under Rear Admiral George Cockburn marched into Washington and deliberately burned the Capitol, the White House, and other federal buildings — a direct assault on the symbols of the young republic. First Lady Dolley Madison arranged for the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington and key government papers to be saved before fleeing. The burning was meant to humiliate; it largely succeeded.

One month later, the British fleet bombarded Fort McHenry outside Baltimore for twenty-five hours. American lawyer Francis Scott Key had gone to the British fleet under a flag of truce to negotiate the release of an American prisoner and was detained aboard ship during the bombardment. Watching through the night, he saw the American flag still flying at dawn on September 14, 1814, and wrote the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner,' with its famous line 'the rockets' red glare' describing the British Congreve rockets.

The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, restored prewar boundaries — status quo ante bellum — and formally resolved nothing about impressment. Two weeks later, Andrew Jackson's forces crushed a veteran British army at the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815, unaware the war was already over. The battle settled nothing legally but produced a wave of national pride that defined how Americans remembered the conflict: a young republic that had stood against the world's greatest military power and survived.

data.title: ERIE CANAL
data.subtitle: Building New York's "Big Ditch," 1817–1825
data.introBody: Albany, 1817. The New York State Legislature has approved the Erie Canal — 363 miles of waterway from the Hudson River to Lake Erie. You are the Canal Commission. The engineering has never been done in America. The money must be found, the workers recruited, and the opposition managed. Eight years stand between you and the most transformative public works project the young republic has ever attempted.
data.trailFeedOpener: Summer 1817: the first shovels break ground near Rome, New York. The Commission convenes to set priorities.

events.title: "Clinton's Folly"
events.text: Critics in the press mock the canal as "Clinton's Ditch" — a boondoggle that will bankrupt the state. Several assemblymen demand the Commission justify every dollar. Public confidence is fragile in these early months.

choices.text: Publish a detailed cost-benefit report for legislators.

choices.text: Ignore the critics. Keep building.
choices.result: The mockery grows louder. Two assemblymen pledge to cut next year's appropriation.

events.title: A Strange Gray Stone
events.text: Workers near Chittenango report a puzzling gray limestone that, when burned and mixed with water, hardens even underwater. Engineer Canvass White has been studying it. If it works, it solves the canal's biggest technical problem: watertight locks.

choices.text: Fund White's experiments. Test the hydraulic cement.
choices.result: The natural cement works. American engineers no longer need to import expensive European materials.

choices.result: Locks are watertight, but costs balloon and critics renew calls to halt the project.

choices.text: Push forward without resolving the problem.
choices.result: Early lock sections leak badly. Benjamin Wright halts construction for emergency repairs.

events.title: Fever in the Work Camps
events.text: A foreman reports malaria and dysentery spreading through the Montezuma Swamp section. Irish laborers are dying at an alarming rate. Slower work or better conditions — the Commission must decide.

choices.text: Halt work in the swamp. Drain and treat the sick.
choices.result: Deaths slow. Workers remember who looked out for them and recruitment improves.

data.historicalContext: The Erie Canal opened in October 1825, eight years after construction began. At 363 miles, it was the longest canal in the Western world. Construction cost approximately $7 million — paid off entirely by toll revenue within nine years. Freight costs from Buffalo to New York City fell from $100 to $10 per ton. Within fifteen years of opening, New York City became the largest city in the Western Hemisphere. The canal transformed the entire interior: western New York farm towns like Rochester exploded in population, grain from Ohio and Indiana reached eastern markets for the first time, and Irish immigrant laborers who built it largely settled in the communities along its banks. The Erie Canal is considered the first great American infrastructure achievement and the engineering school that trained the first generation of American civil engineers.

verdict.good: You built it right. Not just the waterway — the decisions around it. You paid for the surveys, treated the sick workers in the swamp, and built the Lockport locks as Wright designed them. The canal opened in 1825, paid off its seven-million-dollar debt in nine years, and made New York the commercial capital of the continent. You did not do this for yourself. You did it knowing you would not live to see what it became. That is what public works require: people willing to spend on things larger than their own tenure.
verdict.bad: The canal got built, and you were there for it. But the choices you made along the way — the bonus pay instead of the halt, the foreign bankers' terms, the contracts traded for votes — those were not accidents. You treated the workers as a cost to manage and the opposition as a market to buy. The canal still transformed American commerce. The Irish laborers who died in the Montezuma Swamp still died. You stood on the same ground and made different choices than you had to. The waterway does not remember who built it carefully.
verdict.indifferent: You held the Commission's seat for eight years and the canal got finished. That is true. But you kept your head down at every hard moment — waited for critics to tire, let problems drift until they forced themselves, took the easy path when the costly one was the right one. The Erie Canal changed the economic geography of a continent. It required people to choose, repeatedly, to spend and risk and hold the line. You passed through those choices without really making them. The water runs all the same. But you did not build this — you were present while it was built.

data.reviewSummary:
The Erie Canal was authorized by the New York State Legislature in 1817, stretching 363 miles from Buffalo on Lake Erie to Albany on the Hudson River. Governor DeWitt Clinton staked his political career on it despite widespread mockery — critics called it 'Clinton's Folly' — and the Canal Commission had to balance funding, labor, engineering breakthroughs, and relentless political opposition for eight years.

Construction's most important technical breakthrough came when engineer Canvass White discovered a natural hydraulic limestone in central New York that, when burned and mixed with water, hardened even underwater. This natural cement made watertight locks possible without expensive European imports.

The deadliest section was the Montezuma Swamp in central New York, where standing water bred mosquitoes and malaria and dysentery swept through the Irish immigrant labor camps, killing dozens and halting progress. Thousands of Irish laborers built the canal under dangerous conditions throughout the route.

At Lockport, where the canal had to climb sixty feet over the Niagara Escarpment, Chief Engineer Benjamin Wright designed a double flight of five paired locks — celebrated worldwide as a marvel of engineering. The Rochester aqueduct, which carried the canal over the Genesee River on a masonry bridge, drew visitors from across the country.

Financing came through canal bonds backed by toll revenue from completed sections, which allowed New York to avoid dependence on federal or foreign capital. Political opposition, including resistance from state legislators, was overcome by demonstrating that the canal served New York City's merchants as much as upstate landowners.

The canal opened in October 1825. Governor Clinton poured a keg of Lake Erie water into New York Harbor in a ceremony called the Wedding of the Waters, symbolizing the connection between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic. The seven-million-dollar construction cost was paid off entirely by toll revenue within nine years. Freight costs fell from roughly one hundred dollars per ton overland to about ten dollars per ton by water, and New York City quickly became the dominant commercial port in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: The Acre Aftermath — the days following the fall of Acre, August 1191
events.text: Richard has ordered the execution of some 2,700 Muslim prisoners — men taken under terms of surrender whose ransom negotiation has collapsed. Your lord commands you to take part in the killing as a show of unified resolve. Your tent-companion, a veteran knight from Burgundy, tells you flatly: 'We all do this together or the alliance cracks. There is no honorable refusal here — only desertion dressed in clean words.' You have ridden months to be here. These men surrendered. Richard's order is real. The march to Jerusalem cannot begin until this is done.

choices.text: You take your place in the line. The cause is larger than your discomfort, and you will not let your brothers carry alone what all must share.
choices.result: This knight has fused himself to the crusading body — his identity is now inseparable from what the enterprise does, in its worst hours as in its best. He is not cruel; he is committed, and he has paid the price commitment sometimes demands.

choices.text: You step back and refuse the order. You will march, you will fight, you will bleed for Jerusalem — but not this. Whatever it costs you among your brothers, you will not do this.
choices.result: This knight has drawn a line inside himself that the crusade cannot cross — his identity rests on that line. He is not cowardly; he is bounded, and he carries the loneliness of a man who has chosen his own code over the solidarity of the only army that can take him home.

events.title: The Trenches Before Acre
events.text: The siege engineer assigns your company to the forward trench, within crossbow range of the walls. It is miserable, dangerous work. A veteran from Burgundy offers to swap rotations with a lesser knight — for a price.
trivia: Crusader besiegers at Acre dug extensive trench networks to protect against Saladin's relief army attacking from outside.

choices.text: Take the forward trench — no swap, no coin spent.
choices.result: You hold the trench through a brutal week. The men around you notice. A lord's steward marks your name.

choices.text: Pay the swap. Take the safer rotation.
choices.result: The coin buys you a quieter week. The Burgundian says nothing, but his eyes say plenty.

choices.text: Wait to see how the rotation shakes out.
choices.result: You end up in the trench anyway, by default, with no credit for having chosen it.

events.title: Philip's Ships Leave the Harbor
events.text: Acre has fallen. Philip II of France, citing illness, declares he is sailing home to France. His departure strips the crusading host of a third of its knights. Fellow crusaders are furious; some want to formally condemn him before the lords.
trivia: Philip II left the crusade after the fall of Acre in 1191, weakening the army for the march on Jerusalem.

choices.text: Join the public condemnation of Philip's abandonment.
choices.result: You speak openly. Richard's men nod. Philip's remaining allies remember. You have made an enemy across the sea.

choices.text: Say nothing — Philip is still a king.
choices.result: Your silence reads as caution to some, cowardice to others. You keep your options open and lose the room's respect.

choices.text: Quietly broker a final pledge from Philip's remaining captains.
choices.result: You spend coin on wine and talk. Three French knights commit to the march. A small thing — but real.

events.title: The Battle of Arsuf
events.text: On the coastal march south, Saladin's cavalry hammers the flanks without pause. Richard's orders are iron: hold formation, do not charge. Your destrier is screaming. A brother knight breaks ranks and you must decide in seconds.
trivia: At the Battle of Arsuf, September 1191, Richard's ability to hold the Crusader column against Saladin's harassment was critical to the victory.

choices.text: Hold formation. The order is the order.
choices.result: You hold. The torment is immense. When Richard finally gives the charge, you ride with the tide that breaks Saladin's line.

choices.text: Follow the knight who broke — the moment is now.
choices.result: The charge is premature. You expose the flank. Richard's fury is cold and absolute. You survive. Your standing does not.

choices.text: Slow your horse — not quite holding, not quite breaking.
choices.result: The half-measure satisfies no one. You arrive at the rout too late for glory.

events.title: A Prisoner Worth Something
events.text: After a skirmish near Jaffa, you have taken a Saracen officer alive. His armor is fine; his family may pay well. Pushing for more silver carries real risk — the camp is restless and the man speaks some French.
events.leaveText: Take the standard ransom and move on.

attempts.buttonText: Ask a fair price — twenty deniers.
attempts.successText: He agrees at once. Twenty deniers, clean and quick.
attempts.failureText: He has no coin. His comrades buy him back in blades — a night raid on your tent.

attempts.buttonText: Push for thirty-five. He is worth it.
attempts.successText: He pays. You are richer and his dignity is intact.
attempts.failureText: He spits and goes silent. You get nothing. The other knights find it amusing.

attempts.buttonText: Demand everything — horse, armor, and fifty deniers.
attempts.successText: Astonishingly, he agrees. A minor lord — richer than he looked.
attempts.failureText: He refuses and your greed becomes camp gossip. Richard's steward makes a note.

events.title: Conrad's Messenger
events.text: A messenger from Conrad of Montferrat arrives by night. Conrad's claim to the throne of Jerusalem rivals Richard's preferred candidate. The messenger offers gifts and asks for your open support in the lords' council.
trivia: Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan both claimed the throne of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, splitting the Crusader coalition's political will.

choices.text: Refuse the messenger and report the approach to Richard.
choices.result: Richard thanks you with a cold nod and a better billet. Conrad's faction does not forget.

choices.text: Accept the gifts, promise nothing.
choices.result: The gifts are real; the neutrality is not. Word travels. You are now a man who can be bought without being kept.

choices.text: Politely send the messenger away and say nothing to anyone.
choices.result: You keep your distance from the intrigue. Both sides suspect you for it.

events.title: The Settler at the Gate
events.text: A Frankish pilgrim-settler whose family has lived in the Holy Land for two generations begs you to carry a letter to Richard pleading against a negotiated withdrawal. The march has stalled. The leaders are talking of terms. She tells you: 'If you leave without Jerusalem, we are left to whatever comes after you.'
trivia: Richard's 1192 treaty with Saladin secured Christian pilgrim access to Jerusalem but left the city under Muslim control.

choices.text: Carry the letter to Richard's council at personal risk.
choices.result: Richard reads it. He is not moved — the treaty is coming regardless. But the woman knows you tried, and you know it too.

choices.text: Tell her the march is a king's decision, not yours.
choices.result: You are not wrong. You are also not there when the terms are signed and she is left standing at the gates of a city she will never enter.

choices.text: Accept the letter but never deliver it.
choices.result: The coin she presses on you for the errand sits in your purse all the way home. It does not feel like coin.

events.title: The March Down the Coast — the brutal column south from Acre toward Jaffa, September 1191

text.default: You march in silence most days. The Burgundian rides at your shoulder and does not speak of Acre, and neither do you. There is an ease between you that feels earned and also feels like a debt. When Saracen arrows find the men around you and your lord calls the column to hold formation no matter the cost, you hold. You do not flinch. You tell yourself this is what you came for — this discipline, this unity — and you are not wrong. But at night you find yourself counting the days to Jerusalem as though arrival might settle something that has not yet found its name.

You march with a space around you that has nothing to do with distance. The Burgundian rides ahead and does not look back. Three men from your own contingent have not spoken to you since Acre, and you have stopped trying to explain what you cannot quite articulate even to yourself. When the Saracen arrows come and your lord calls the column to hold, you hold — fiercely, as though the holding proves something. You do not know whether you are proving it to your brothers or to yourself. Jerusalem is still ahead, and you are still here, and you are not sure whether that is enough.

choices.text: Go on.

events.title: The Council at Beit Nuba — Richard halts the advance on Jerusalem, January 1192

text.default: The barons argue for two days. Richard will not march on Jerusalem without supply lines that do not exist. Men around you curse him for a coward, and you say nothing. You have learned what it costs to question the man the cause runs through. When the order comes to turn back, you turn back. You tell yourself this is the same discipline that held the column together on the coast road. You are not sure you are wrong. You are also not sure you are right. The city remains unbroken on the horizon, and you ride away from it with your lord, which is what you decided, in the end, you were.

The barons argue for two days. Richard will not march on Jerusalem without supply lines that do not exist. You listen and feel, for the first time in months, something clarify. You rode out for Jerusalem. Not for Richard, not for the alliance, not for the political mathematics of a campaign. When voices around you begin to whisper that a knight of conscience might carry the argument for pressing on — might speak where others calculate — you feel the old pressure return: what do you owe the cause, and what does the cause owe you? The city is still there. You have not yet decided whether that means the story is unfinished, or whether it only means the world does not settle its debts.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Master Bertrand
sages.title: Crusader Siege Engineer
sages.bio: A veteran military engineer who has served in three sieges, Master Bertrand oversees the trebuchets and mangonels before Acre's walls. He speaks little of God and much of stone, weight, and trajectory.
sages.greeting: You find him at dawn, measuring the angle of a trebuchet arm with a knotted cord. He doesn't look up.
sages.advice: "Acre's walls are two yards thick. You don't fight stone — you starve it. Cut their supply line from the sea and the walls open themselves."

question.question: What was the main purpose of a trebuchet in medieval siege warfare?
choices: To launch soldiers over walls
To hurl heavy stones and break down fortifications
To carry supplies across rivers
To signal allied armies with fire
question.explanation: A trebuchet used a counterweight to fling heavy stones at walls, gates, and towers, battering them until they collapsed or the garrison surrendered.
question.teksRef: Social Studies 7th — Medieval warfare and technology

sages.name: Richard I of England
sages.title: King of England, Commander of the Crusade
sages.bio: Richard I, called the Lionheart, is the dominant military mind of the crusading coalition. He took the cross after years of political warfare at home and arrived in the Holy Land with the most organized force in Christendom. His anger is cold; his praise is rare and worth everything.
sages.greeting: He summons you after the march from Arsuf. His tent smells of iron and horse. He watches you the way a hawk watches a field.
sages.advice: "Every man who rides with me fights for God, for England, and for order — in that sequence. The moment you decide your honor matters more than the column, you are not a soldier. You are a liability."

question.question: Why did Richard I take the city of Acre before marching toward Jerusalem?
choices: Acre was the birthplace of Jesus
Acre was a key port needed to supply the march inland
Saladin had his headquarters in Acre
The Pope ordered him to begin at Acre specifically
question.explanation: Acre was the most important port on the Palestinian coast. Controlling it gave the Crusader army a secure supply base and harbor for reinforcements and provisions before the difficult inland march.
question.teksRef: Social Studies 7th — The Crusades: strategy and logistics

sages.name: Saladin's Envoy
sages.title: Emissary of Salah ad-Din, Sultan of Egypt and Syria
sages.bio: Saladin does not come himself — he sends an educated courtier who speaks French with a slight Damascene accent and carries terms in a sealed letter. The envoy is courteous, precise, and utterly unyielding on the question of Jerusalem.
sages.greeting: He meets you at a designated point between the lines, alone except for a translator. He bows exactly as much as courtesy requires.
sages.advice: "The Sultan does not hate you. He asks only that you understand: Jerusalem has been Islamic since 637. Your God and ours are not strangers to this city. The Sultan offers terms that preserve your pilgrims' access. Consider what a second siege of Jerusalem would cost you."

question.question: What did Saladin's 1187 victory at the Battle of Hattin allow him to do?
choices: Capture the entire coast of the Mediterranean
Retake Jerusalem and end the First Crusader Kingdom
Defeat the Byzantine Empire
Force Richard to leave the Holy Land immediately
question.explanation: At the Battle of Hattin in 1187, Saladin destroyed the main Crusader army and captured their king. This allowed him to retake Jerusalem, ending the First Kingdom of Jerusalem and triggering the Third Crusade.
question.teksRef: Social Studies 7th — The Crusades: causes and Islamic response

It kept Saladin's cavalry from splitting the column
It conserved water for the march

Emperor

Greek fire

choices: Tribute
Ransom

eventTrivia.fact: Ransom — paying for a captured enemy's release — was standard medieval practice and a significant source of income for knights.

eventTrivia.fact: 'Deus vult' means 'God wills it.' The phrase was reportedly shouted by the crowd at the Council of Clermont in 1095 when Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade.
