choices: To pay taxes to the Pope
To serve his lord's command and hold his place in the battle line
To negotiate treaties with Muslim leaders
To write letters home describing the campaign
eventTrivia.fact: A knight's core duty was obedience to his lord and discipline in formation. Breaking ranks or disobeying a command in battle could endanger the entire army.

data.historicalContext: The Third Crusade (1189–1192) ended without Crusader forces retaking Jerusalem. Richard I and Saladin signed a treaty in September 1192: Christians would have safe pilgrim access to Jerusalem, but the city remained under Muslim control. Richard never set foot in Jerusalem. Saladin died in 1193. The Crusader states survived on the coast for another century, but the dream of a Christian Jerusalem would not be achieved in this generation.

verdict.good: You rode out a knight and came back one. Every time the choice was costly you held your ground — in the trench, on the march, before the settler's gate. It did not save Jerusalem. The treaty came regardless, and the pilgrim woman is still standing at the gates of a city no treaty quite opens. Richard came home famous. Saladin came home with Jerusalem. You came home with a name you can say without wincing, which in 1192 is rarer than it sounds.
verdict.bad: You found the safe side of every choice and stayed there. The coin was real; the standing you traded for it was not. The trench got held by someone else. The settler's letter went undelivered. The march went where it was always going, and you went with it, comfortable and unremarkable. You came back from a holy war having cost it nothing — which means it cost you nothing, which means you were never really there.
verdict.indifferent: You were present. That is the most that can be said. When the choices came you took the one that asked least of you, and the crusade moved around you like a river around a stone. The trench got dug, the battle got fought, the treaty got signed — you were there for all of it and shaped none of it. A thousand men made this campaign. You passed through it. History did not record where you stood, because where you stood was never quite anywhere.

data.reviewSummary: The Third Crusade began because Saladin — Sultan of Egypt and Syria — destroyed the main Crusader army at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 and retook Jerusalem, ending the First Kingdom of Jerusalem. Pope Gregory VIII called for a new crusade, and Richard I of England joined Philip II of France as co-leaders of the campaign. The two kings arrived at the port city of Acre in 1191. Acre was the most important harbor on the Palestinian coast, and the Crusaders needed it to supply their army with food, equipment, and reinforcements. After a long siege using trebuchets — counterweighted war machines that hurled heavy stones to break fortifications — Acre fell in July 1191. Philip II, citing illness, promptly sailed home to France, stripping the host of a third of its knights and leaving Richard to continue with a weakened force. On the brutal coastal march south toward Jerusalem, Saladin's cavalry — armed with composite bows — harassed the column constantly, trying to goad the Crusaders into a premature charge. At the Battle of Arsuf in September 1191, Richard held his army in tight formation under relentless fire until the decisive moment, breaking Saladin's line. The internal politics of the crusade were nearly as damaging as Saladin himself. Conrad of Montferrat's rival claim to the throne of the Kingdom of Jerusalem split the coalition. Richard twice halted the advance on Jerusalem — most critically at Beit Nuba in January 1192 — because his advisors argued that even if taken, the city could not be held: supply lines were overextended and crusaders would return home after the pilgrimage, leaving too few to garrison it. In September 1192, Richard and Saladin signed a treaty. Jerusalem remained under Muslim control. Christian pilgrims received guaranteed safe access to the holy sites. Richard never entered Jerusalem. Saladin died in 1193. The Crusader states held the coast for another century, but the dream of a reconquered Jerusalem died here.

data.title: ROAD TO CALIFORNIA
data.subtitle: Oklahoma to the Central Valley, 1936
data.introBody: 1936. The bank has posted the notice. The fields are buried under red drifts, the livestock is gone, and there is maybe forty dollars in your pocket. You have loaded the family onto a groaning flatbed and pointed it west on Route 66. California is 1,500 miles away. You have never been that far from home in your life.
data.trailFeedOpener: Spring 1936: the truck coughs to life in the predawn dark, and Oklahoma falls away behind you.

events.title: The night before departure — the truck is loaded past its limit, the radiator is already weeping, and Grandpa Tipton has had another spell. He cannot walk unassisted. His sister's boy, Denny, is running a fever that won't break.
events.text: Your wife says nothing, but you see her doing the same counting you are. There is maybe forty dollars between this family and the ditch. The truck cannot carry this weight over the mountains — you know it the way you know weather. Two of your people may not survive the road. Your brother says he can stay behind with the old man and the sick boy, find work locally, catch up later — you both know 'later' is a word that means never in times like these. You have to decide before dawn.

choices.text: We all go. We started as a family and we end as one — I will not look my brother in the eye and call him the one we left. We find a way to make the truck hold. We make the road work for all of us or none of us.
choices.result: He refuses to become a man who calculates the worth of his own kin. The family's wholeness is the thing he is protecting — without it, he isn't sure what the journey is even for.

choices.text: Grandpa and Denny stay with Roy. I will send money the moment there's money to send. This is the only way I can look the ones who make it in the eye someday — because I gave them a real chance instead of a beautiful lie.
choices.result: He accepts a wound that will not close — that to protect some of his people he must become the man who sorted them. He does not pretend it is anything other than what it is.

events.title: Black Blizzard
events.text: A wall of darkness rolls in from the north — a black blizzard, the sky turned to dirt. The truck's engine chokes on the dust. You can pull over and wait it out or push through before the road disappears.

choices.text: Pull over, wet rags over the faces, wait it out.
choices.result: The storm passes in two hours. The kids stop coughing, and your wife squeezes your hand. The truck starts clean.

choices.text: Keep driving — every hour stopped is money gone.
choices.result: The air filter packs with red dirt. You crawl the last miles into the next town, pay a mechanic three dollars to clean it out, and the kids cough for two days.

trivia: The worst dust storms of the 1930s could bury cars and livestock overnight.
Families stuffed wet rags under doors and over faces to filter the choking air.

events.title: Roadside Camp
events.text: You pull off Route 66 near a dry wash. A dozen other Okie families are already camped here — battered trucks, mattresses tied on top, children running barefoot. One family has a sick toddler and no money for a doctor.

choices.text: Share your water and two cans of food with them.
choices.result: The mother thanks you without words, just a long look. Your kids watch and say nothing. Your wife counts the cans that are left.

choices.text: Stay separate — you cannot afford to feed someone else's children.
choices.result: You save the cans. The toddler's crying carries across the wash all night. Your older boy doesn't speak to you at breakfast.

choices.text: Trade information — where to find water, what towns to avoid.
choices.result: They tell you Needles has a standpipe for free water. You tell them about the mechanic in Amarillo who won't cheat Okies. Something is exchanged that costs nothing.

trivia: Route 66 ran from Chicago to Los Angeles and became the main migration corridor for Dust Bowl families.
Migrant families often shared information about work, water, and hostile towns along the route.

events.title: The Arizona Line
events.text: A state agricultural inspector waves you to the shoulder. He says he needs to check for pests. He eyes the family, the mattresses, the cast-iron stove bungeed to the truck bed. You can tell he is deciding whether to let you through at all.

choices.text: Answer steady and polite — yes sir, no sir, just passing through.
choices.result: He waves you through after ten minutes. Your jaw aches from holding your face still.

choices.text: Slip him two dollars to wave you through fast.
choices.result: He pockets it without looking at you and waves at the next car. Two dollars gone. The family is through.

choices.text: Ask him plainly what law says he can stop an American family.
choices.result: He makes you wait an hour in the sun and searches every box on the truck. He finds nothing. He lets you go. The kids saw you not back down.

trivia: California and Arizona both attempted to restrict migrant entry in the 1930s, with local officers sometimes turning back cars at borders.
These informal blockades were often called 'bum blockades' and had questionable legal standing.

events.title: The Mojave Stalls
events.text: The radiator blows a stream of steam on the Mojave Desert road. The temperature gauge is pinned. In this heat, a stopped engine can cook itself dead. A passing truck driver offers to tow you to a salvage yard ten miles back — for five dollars.

choices.text: Pay the five dollars. Get towed back.
choices.result: The salvage man finds a cracked hose. Two dollars more and it's patched. You lose a day but the engine runs cool.

choices.text: Wait for the engine to cool, patch it with tape and wire.
choices.result: The tape holds for fifty miles. The hiss comes back at nightfall. You limp into Needles, the engine knocking.

outcomes.result: The tape holds for fifty miles, then fails. You coast into Needles and pay a mechanic at dark.
By some miracle the patch holds all the way to Needles. The hose gives out in the parking lot of the filling station.

choices.text: Push through. Drive fast, hope the engine makes it.
choices.result: The engine seizes three miles from Needles. You push the truck off the road and walk in the 105-degree heat. Your youngest cries the whole way.

trivia: The Mojave Desert crossing was one of the most dangerous stretches of Route 66 for migrants in old vehicles.
Many families traveled the desert at night to spare their engines from the heat.

events.title: The Handbills Lied
events.text: The handbill said 800 workers needed — good wages, steady work. When you pull into the labor camp outside Bakersfield, there are three thousand people ahead of you. A contractor walks the line calling out numbers. He is only taking sixty.
events.imageSearchQuery: Farm Security Administration Kern County migrant camp 1936

choices.text: Get in line and wait your turn with everyone else.
choices.result: You wait six hours. You don't get picked. But you didn't push anyone out. Tonight the family eats the last of the salt pork.

data.historicalContext: Between 1930 and 1940, over 2.5 million people fled the Dust Bowl states for California. Decades of deep plowing had destroyed the native grasslands of the Southern Plains; when drought came, the topsoil simply blew away. In California, migrants found labor oversupply engineered by growers distributing misleading handbills, piece-rate wages that did not cover food, and active hostility from local governments. FSA camps like the one at Arvin offered a fragment of dignity — clean water, schooling, elected self-governance — but could not absorb the wave of desperate families. The Dust Bowl and the Depression together produced the largest internal migration in American history to that point.

verdict.good: You chose the harder road every time the easier one was right there. You shared food when you had little to spare, you stood your ground when it cost you an hour in the Arizona sun, you paid the camp fee and fed the family next to yours even when your own kids went to bed hungry. It didn't make California fair. The handbills still lied, the foreman still took sixty out of three thousand, and the land back in Oklahoma is still buried under six feet of dust. But you carried something across the desert that a lot of men dropped somewhere in New Mexico — the belief that the people beside you were your people too. History doesn't record your name. It records what Okies did, together, when the country turned its back. You were one of the ones who held.
verdict.bad: You did the math on every choice, and the math always came out the same: yours first. You drove through the blizzard and paid the mechanic, you slipped the inspector two dollars, you took the camp spot and didn't look at the family in the car. None of it was monstrous — it was just the arithmetic of a man who decided early that survival was personal. You made it. A lot of Okies didn't. The ones who didn't weren't weaker than you; they were unlucky, or they kept stopping to help people, which turned out to be expensive. You can live with the choices you made. Most of them you've already stopped thinking about. That's probably how it works.
verdict.indifferent: You kept your head down, took the obvious call, and let every hard choice resolve itself. You waited out the inspection because it was easier than fighting it. You traded information instead of food because it cost nothing. You slept in the truck to save the money and told yourself it was practical. Nobody got hurt by you. Nobody got helped much either. You crossed one of the hardest migrations in American history and came out the other side about the same as you went in — not worse, not better, just through. Three thousand people stood in that labor line and only sixty got picked. The ones beside you were just as hungry as you were. You were there. You passed through. The road asked you something and you never quite answered.

data.reviewSummary: In 1936, the Southern Plains were in the grip of a catastrophe years in the making. Since World War I, farmers had plowed up millions of acres of native grassland to plant wheat, destroying the root systems that had held the soil in place for millennia. When drought arrived in the 1930s, there was nothing to anchor the topsoil. Nearly 300 major dust storms swept across the region during that decade, burying farms and livestock under walls of black and red dirt. Families stuffed wet rags under doors and over faces to breathe. The worst storms carried dust as far as Washington D.C. — a fact that finally forced Congress into action. On the strength of that moment, Hugh Hammond Bennett, a federal soil scientist who had spent years warning of exactly this collapse, secured passage of the Soil Conservation Act in 1935, becoming the first chief of the new Soil Conservation Service. His agency planted trees and taught farmers how to restore what decades of deep plowing had destroyed. Across the Southern Plains, more than 2.5 million people eventually left for California, most of them following Route 66 — a road that ran from Chicago to Los Angeles and became known as the Mother Road. California growers had printed and distributed handbills advertising far more farm work than actually existed, drawing desperate families into a deliberately oversupplied labor market where piece-rate wages could be set near nothing. When migrants arrived, they found county officials and informal border blockades trying to turn them back, and private labor camps with squalid conditions and no rights. The Farm Security Administration responded by building camps like the one at Arvin, near Bakersfield — managed by Tom Collins — where migrants had access to clean water, sanitation, schooling, and elected resident councils to govern themselves. FSA photographer Dorothea Lange documented migrant life across California, including her 1936 photograph of Florence Owens Thompson, a 32-year-old mother of seven stranded at a pea-pickers camp in Nipomo, California. That image, called 'Migrant Mother,' became the defining face of the Depression and shaped public support for New Deal relief programs. The New Deal's Agricultural Adjustment Act paid farmers to reduce production to stabilize crop prices, while the Civilian Conservation Corps employed roughly 3 million young men planting trees and building erosion controls. For tenant farmers and sharecroppers, however, most of these payments went to landowners, not to the people who worked the land.

data.historicalContext: The Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804–1806) was the first American overland expedition to the Pacific Coast and back. Commissioned by President Jefferson after the Louisiana Purchase, the Corps of Discovery mapped over 3,700 miles of territory, documented hundreds of plant and animal species, and made contact with dozens of Native nations. All but one member of the Corps returned alive. Their maps and journals opened the American West to settlement, trade, and ultimately the displacement of the Native peoples who had guided and fed them.

verdict.good: You led honestly. You listened to Sacagawea, traded fairly with the nations you met, and put the mission above your own comfort. The Corps came home. Every single man. That almost never happens. The journals you carried back changed what Americans thought possible — and you earned the right to have carried them. History remembers the expedition as a triumph. You helped make it one, and you know what it cost the people who fed and guided you. Hold that.
verdict.bad: You got through. The Columbia, the Rockies, the Missouri — all of it. But every time a Native nation offered trust, you measured what you could take from it. You demanded horses instead of earning them. You pressed on when patience was owed. The Corps made it back, and the maps they brought opened the West. What came after — the settlers, the displacement, the broken agreements — you didn't cause it alone. But you practiced the thinking that made it possible. The expedition was a success. So were you. Think about what those two things mean together.
verdict.indifferent: You made it to the Pacific. You came back. The journals got written, the maps got drawn, and history called it one of the great American achievements. You were there for all of it and took the easy call every time one was offered. When the Shoshone stood in front of you, you neither gave nor took — you waited. When the Bitterroot nearly broke the Corps, you let someone else decide. The expedition succeeded because Lewis and Clark and Sacagawea carried it. You traveled with them. That is not the same thing as what they did.

data.reviewSummary:
In the spring of 1804, President Thomas Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to lead the Corps of Discovery up the Missouri River and across the continent to the Pacific Ocean. Jefferson had just completed the Louisiana Purchase — doubling the size of the United States — and he needed the land mapped, its peoples documented, and a practical route to the Pacific found for trade. The Corps numbered about 33 men and set off from Camp Dubois near St. Louis.

That first winter, the Corps stopped near a cluster of Mandan villages in present-day North Dakota and built Fort Mandan. Wintering there proved critical: the Mandan shared food, route knowledge, and trade connections. It was also where Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, and her husband Toussaint Charbonneau joined the expedition as interpreters. Sacagawea's role became essential — she communicated with Native peoples along the way and, most critically, helped the Corps obtain horses from the Shoshone. The Shoshone chief, Cameahwait, turned out to be her own brother. That reunion secured the horses the Corps needed to cross the Rocky Mountains.

The Bitterroot crossing was the expedition's most dangerous stretch — eleven days of snow, fallen timber, and near-starvation. Nez Perce guides helped lead the Corps through. On the far side, they built canoes and ran the Columbia River to the Pacific, reaching Fort Clatsop in November 1805. The return journey the following year brought the Corps safely back to St. Louis in September 1806. All but one member survived the entire journey.

The expedition produced the first reliable maps of the Louisiana Territory and Pacific Northwest, described hundreds of plant and animal species, and made contact with dozens of Native nations. That knowledge encouraged American settlement and trade — and the westward expansion that followed reshaped the lives of the Native peoples who had guided and fed the Corps along the way.
